His performance in the minors was solid, with a career minor league batting average of .265, and he demonstrated strong defensive abilities behind the plate.

Nieves made his MLB debut on April 19, 2002, with the San Diego Padres, appearing in 13 games that season. Though his time with the Padres was limited, he gained valuable experience at the major league level. In 2003, he was traded to the Anaheim Angels as part of a deal that sent pitcher Jason Middlebrook to the Padres. Nieves spent most of the 2003 season with the Salt Lake Stingers, the Angels' Triple-A affiliate, before being called up for a brief stint in September, appearing in four games.

After the 2003 season, Nieves was selected by the Washington Nationals in the Rule 5 Draft. He spent the 2004 season with the Nationals, serving as a backup catcher and appearing in 40 games, posting a .254 batting average. His time in Washington was short-lived, as he was designated for assignment in 2005 and later claimed off waivers by the New York Yankees. Nieves spent most of the 2005 and 2006 seasons in the Yankees' minor league system with the Columbus Clippers, though he did appear in 11 games for the Yankees in 2005.

In 2007, Nieves signed with the Seattle Mariners and spent the season with their Triple-A affiliate, the Tacoma Rainiers. He was called up to the Mariners in September 2007, appearing in 11 games. The following year, Nieves became the Mariners' primary backup catcher, playing in 67 games and batting .251 with two home runs and 16 RBIs. His defensive skills, particularly his ability to control the running game, made him a valuable asset to the team.

Nieves signed with the Milwaukee Brewers in 2009 but spent most of the season with their Triple-A affiliate, the Nashville Sounds. He was called up in September and appeared in six games for the Brewers. In 2010, he returned to the Nationals, where he served as a backup catcher for two seasons. During this time, he played in 88 games, batting .240 with three home runs and 18 RBIs. One of his most memorable moments came on June 28, 2011, when he hit a walk-off single in the 12th inning to give the Nationals a 2-1 victory over the Chicago White Sox.

In 2012, Nieves signed with the Colorado Rockies and played in 29 games before being released in August. He then signed with the Arizona Diamondbacks, appearing in 12 games for them that season. Nieves spent the 2013 season with the Philadelphia Phillies, serving as a backup catcher and playing in 42 games. His final MLB season came in 2015 with the San Diego Padres, where he appeared in 25 games, batting .247.

Over his 12-year MLB career, Nieves played in 348 games, compiling a .241 batting average with 13 home runs and 90 RBIs. Known for his defensive prowess, he threw out 28% of base stealers during his career, which was above the league average for catchers at the time. After retiring as a player, Nieves remained involved in baseball, working as a catching instructor and minor league coach. He served as the bullpen catcher for the Washington Nationals in 2016 and later worked in player development roles within the organization.

In his personal life, Nieves has been married to his wife, Wanda, since 2001, and the couple has three children. He has remained active in charitable work, particularly in his native Puerto Rico, where he has supported youth baseball programs and disaster relief efforts. Nieves' career, though not marked by flashy statistics, was defined by his reliability, professionalism, and dedication to the game.

title: Akbar Hossain
text:
Akbar Hossain was born on March 15, 1945, in the small village of Char Fasson, located in the Bhola District of what was then East Pakistan (now Bangladesh). His parents, Mohammad Hossain and Ayesha Begum, were modest farmers, and Akbar was the eldest of six siblings. Growing up in a rural setting, he attended the local primary school in Char Fasson before moving to Bhola Government High School for his secondary education, where he completed his matriculation in 1962 with first division marks. His academic excellence earned him a scholarship to study at Dhaka College, where he enrolled in the science program, graduating in 1964 with distinction.

Hossain’s higher education began at the University of Dhaka, where he pursued a Bachelor of Science in Chemistry, graduating in 1967. His passion for science led him to secure a government scholarship to study abroad, and in 1968, he enrolled at the University of Manchester in the United Kingdom. There, he earned a Master of Science in Analytical Chemistry in 1970, followed by a Ph.D. in the same field in 1973. His doctoral research focused on the development of spectroscopic methods for environmental analysis, a field that would later define much of his professional career.

Upon returning to Bangladesh in 1974, Hossain joined the Bangladesh Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (BCSIR) as a senior scientific officer. His early work involved developing cost-effective methods for water and soil testing, which were critical in a country grappling with widespread pollution and agricultural challenges. In 1978, he was promoted to principal scientific officer and led a team that established the first national laboratory for environmental monitoring in Dhaka. This facility, inaugurated on December 12, 1980, became a cornerstone for pollution control efforts in Bangladesh, providing data that influenced government policies on industrial waste management.

One of Hossain’s most significant contributions came in the 1980s when he led a research project on arsenic contamination in groundwater. His team’s findings, published in the *Journal of Environmental Science and Health* in 1985, were among the first to document the severity of arsenic poisoning in Bangladesh. The study revealed that over 20% of tube wells in certain regions, particularly in the southern districts, contained arsenic levels exceeding the World Health Organization’s safety limit of 50 micrograms per liter. This discovery prompted the government to launch a nationwide testing program in 1987, ultimately leading to the identification of millions of contaminated wells. For his work, Hossain received the Bangladesh Science Academy Gold Medal in 1989, one of the country’s highest scientific honors.

In 1990, Hossain was appointed director of the Institute of Environmental Science at the University of Rajshahi, a position he held until 1998. During this time, he expanded the institute’s research capabilities, securing funding from international organizations such as the World Health Organization and the United Nations Development Programme. Under his leadership, the institute conducted a landmark study on the health impacts of arsenic exposure, which was published in *The Lancet* in 1996. The study, which involved over 12,000 participants across 10 districts, provided conclusive evidence linking arsenic-contaminated water to skin lesions, cancers, and cardiovascular diseases. This research was instrumental in shaping the government’s response to the crisis, including the installation of deep tube wells and the promotion of alternative water sources.

Hossain’s later career saw him take on advisory roles in both national and international forums. From 1999 to 2005, he served as a technical advisor to the Bangladesh Department of Public Health Engineering, where he helped design and implement the National Arsenic Mitigation Policy, adopted in 2004. He also worked as a consultant for the World Bank, contributing to projects aimed at improving water quality in South Asia. In 2006, he was awarded the Ekushey Padak, Bangladesh’s second-highest civilian award, for his contributions to science and public health.

In his later years, Hossain remained active in academia and advocacy. He joined the faculty of North South University in Dhaka in 2007 as a professor of environmental science, where he taught until his retirement in 2015. Even after retiring, he continued to write and speak on environmental issues, publishing over 150 research papers and several books, including *Arsenic in Groundwater: Poisoning and Risk Assessment* (2010). He also served as a board member for the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association and was a frequent commentator on national media regarding pollution and climate change.

Akbar Hossain passed away on November 3, 2021, in Dhaka at the age of 76, following complications from a stroke. He was survived by his wife, Dr. Fatema Hossain, a physician, and their two children, both of whom followed careers in science and medicine. His legacy endures through the countless lives saved by his research and the policies it inspired, as well as the generations of scientists he mentored. In recognition of his contributions, the government of Bangladesh posthumously awarded him the Independence Day Award in 2022, the nation’s highest civilian honor.

title: Abdelhamid Shabana
text:
Abdelhamid Shabana was an Egyptian footballer and coach, born on March 15, 1934, in the coastal city of Alexandria, Egypt. He grew up in a working-class neighborhood, where his passion for football developed early. As a child, Shabana played in local youth leagues, showcasing a natural talent for the game. His family, though not wealthy, supported his athletic pursuits, recognizing his potential. By the age of 16, he had joined the youth ranks of Al-Ittihad Alexandria Club, one of the oldest and most storied football clubs in Egypt, founded in 1914.

Shabana’s professional career began in 1952 when he was promoted to Al-Ittihad’s senior team at the age of 18. He quickly established himself as a versatile and skilled player, capable of playing multiple positions, though he was most effective as a midfielder. His technical ability, vision, and leadership on the field made him a key figure in the club’s successes during the 1950s. Between 1952 and 1965, Shabana played over 250 matches for Al-Ittihad, scoring 47 goals. During this period, the club won the Egyptian Cup twice, in 1954 and 1959, and finished as runners-up in the Egyptian Premier League on three occasions (1953–54, 1957–58, and 1963–64).

Shabana’s international career with the Egyptian national team was equally notable. He made his debut for Egypt in 1955 at the age of 21, during a friendly match against Sudan in Cairo. Over the next decade, he earned 32 caps and scored 8 goals for his country. One of his most memorable performances came in the 1957 Africa Cup of Nations, held in Sudan, where Egypt won the tournament. Shabana played a crucial role in the final against Ethiopia, assisting in two of Egypt’s four goals in a 4-0 victory. He also represented Egypt in the 1959 and 1962 editions of the tournament, though the team did not repeat its earlier success.

After retiring as a player in 1965 at the age of 31, Shabana transitioned into coaching. His first major coaching role came in 1967 when he was appointed as the head coach of Al-Ittihad Alexandria, the club where he had spent his entire playing career. Under his leadership, the team achieved moderate success, finishing third in the Egyptian Premier League in the 1968–69 season. He remained with Al-Ittihad until 1972, after which he took a brief hiatus from coaching. In 1974, he returned to the sidelines as the assistant coach of the Egyptian national team, working under the legendary Hungarian coach, Nándor Hidegkuti. During this period, Egypt qualified for the 1974 African Cup of Nations, though the team was eliminated in the group stage.

Shabana’s coaching career also included stints with several other Egyptian clubs. From 1976 to 1978, he managed Smouha SC, another Alexandria-based club, helping them secure promotion to the Egyptian Premier League in 1977. He later coached Tersana SC from 1979 to 1981, guiding the team to a fourth-place finish in the 1980–81 season. His final coaching position was with Al-Masry SC in Port Said, where he worked from 1982 to 1984 before retiring from professional football entirely.

In his later years, Shabana remained involved in football as a mentor and advisor, often invited to speak at coaching clinics and youth development programs in Alexandria. He was also a regular attendee at Al-Ittihad matches, where he was revered as a club legend. Despite his contributions to Egyptian football, Shabana lived modestly, avoiding the limelight. He passed away on November 12, 2009, at the age of 75, in Alexandria, due to complications from diabetes. His funeral was attended by hundreds of former players, coaches, and fans, a testament to his enduring legacy in Egyptian football. Shabana’s name is still celebrated in Alexandria, where he is remembered as one of the city’s greatest footballers and a symbol of its rich sporting history.

title: Jemima Goldsmith
text:
Jemima Goldsmith was born Jemima Marcelle Khan on January 30, 1974, in London, England, into one of Britain’s most prominent and wealthy families. Her father, Sir James Goldsmith, was a billionaire financier and founder of the Referendum Party, while her mother, Lady Annabel Goldsmith (née Vane-Tempest-Stewart), was a socialite and the daughter of the 8th Marquess of Londonderry. Jemima was the eldest of three children, with brothers Zac and Ben Goldsmith, both of whom later became prominent politicians. She grew up between the family’s estates in England, France, and Spain, receiving an elite education at the prestigious Francis Holland School in London before studying English at the University of Bristol, though she did not complete her degree.

In 1994, at the age of 20, Jemima met Imran Khan, the celebrated Pakistani cricketer and future prime minister, during a charity cricket match in London. Their relationship developed quickly, and they married on May 16, 1995, in a high-profile ceremony in Paris, followed by a traditional Islamic *nikah* in Lahore, Pakistan. The marriage thrust Jemima into the global spotlight, particularly in Pakistan, where Imran Khan was a national hero. She converted to Islam before the wedding and adopted the name Jemima Goldsmith Khan, though she later dropped "Goldsmith" in public life. The couple had two sons, Sulaiman Isa Khan (born 1996) and Kasim Khan (born 1999), and divided their time between London and Lahore.

During her marriage, Jemima became deeply involved in Pakistani society and philanthropy. She learned Urdu and worked to support her husband’s political ambitions, including his founding of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party in 1996. She also established the *Jemima Khan Relief Fund* in 1998, which provided aid to Afghan refugees in Pakistan following the Taliban’s rise to power. In 2003, she launched *Vanity Fair Pakistan*, a short-lived but culturally significant magazine that aimed to showcase Pakistani talent and perspectives. Despite her efforts to integrate, her marriage faced intense scrutiny, with critics in Pakistan often targeting her Western background. After nine years, Jemima and Imran Khan divorced on June 22, 2004, citing the strains of public life and cultural differences, though they remained on amicable terms.

Following her divorce, Jemima returned to London and reinvented herself as a writer, producer, and activist. In 2005, she became an associate editor at *The Independent* and later contributed to publications like *The Sunday Times*, *The New Statesman*, and *The Spectator*, often writing about politics, human rights, and South Asian affairs. She also worked as a documentary producer, co-founding the production company *Instinct Productions* in 2008. One of her most notable projects was the 2010 documentary *We Steal Secrets: The Story of WikiLeaks*, directed by Alex Gibney, in which she served as an executive producer. The film explored the controversial activities of Julian Assange and WikiLeaks, reflecting her long-standing interest in transparency and free speech.

Jemima’s activism extended to human rights causes, particularly those involving women and children. In 2011, she became a UNICEF UK ambassador, advocating for education and protection for vulnerable children worldwide. She also supported the *Malala Fund*, founded by Malala Yousafzai, and campaigned against child marriage. In 2013, she was appointed a trustee of the *Elton John AIDS Foundation*, further cementing her role in global humanitarian efforts. Her political engagement continued as well; in 2016, she publicly supported Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, despite her family’s traditional ties to the Conservative Party, and later criticized the UK government’s handling of Brexit.

In her personal life, Jemima had a long-term relationship with British journalist and broadcaster Rebekah Brooks, which lasted from 2006 to 2010. She later dated American actor Hugh Grant from 2011 to 2014. In 2015, she briefly returned to the public eye in Pakistan when Imran Khan, then a rising political figure, faced allegations of corruption. Jemima defended him in a series of tweets, reaffirming their friendship and his integrity. By the late 2010s, she had largely stepped back from frontline politics but remained active in media and philanthropy. In 2020, she launched *Jemima Khan Jewellery*, a sustainable jewelry brand that donates a portion of profits to charitable causes.

As of 2024, Jemima Khan resides in London and continues her work in journalism, film production, and advocacy. She remains a vocal supporter of human rights, particularly in South Asia, and maintains a close relationship with her sons, who have occasionally appeared in public with their father. Despite the challenges of her high-profile marriages and public life, she has carved out a distinct identity as a writer, producer, and philanthropist, leveraging her platform to effect change while navigating the complexities of her personal and professional legacy.

title: Roxana Miranda
text:
Roxana Miranda Rupailaf was born on August 28, 1966, in Osorno, a city in the Los Lagos Region of southern Chile. She grew up in a working-class family, the daughter of José Miranda and María Rupailaf, both of Mapuche-Huilliche descent. Her upbringing in the culturally rich but economically marginalized region of La Araucanía deeply influenced her later activism and political career. Miranda attended local public schools, where she developed an early interest in social justice, inspired by the struggles of Indigenous communities and the urban poor in Chile during the late 20th century.

After completing her secondary education, Miranda moved to Santiago in the late 1980s to pursue higher education. She enrolled at the Universidad de Santiago de Chile (USACH), where she studied social work. During this period, Chile was transitioning from the military dictatorship of Augusto Pinochet (1973–1990) to a democratic government, and Miranda became actively involved in student movements advocating for human rights and social reforms. She joined the Communist Youth of Chile and later the Communist Party, aligning herself with leftist causes that sought to address inequality and Indigenous rights.

Miranda’s political career began in earnest in the 1990s. In 1992, she was elected as a councilor for the municipality of La Pintana, a working-class commune in Santiago, representing the Communist Party. She served in this role until 2000, focusing on housing, education, and social welfare programs for low-income families. Her work in La Pintana earned her recognition as a grassroots leader, and in 2000, she was elected mayor of the same municipality, becoming one of the few Indigenous women to hold such a position in Chile at the time. She served two consecutive terms, from 2000 to 2008, during which she implemented policies aimed at reducing poverty, improving public housing, and expanding access to education. Under her leadership, La Pintana saw a 15% reduction in extreme poverty rates, according to municipal records.

In 2009, Miranda ran for a seat in the Chamber of Deputies, Chile’s lower house of Congress, representing District 28, which includes La Pintana and other southern Santiago communes. She won the election with 22.3% of the vote, becoming the first Mapuche woman to serve in the Chilean Congress. During her term (2010–2014), she focused on labor rights, Indigenous land claims, and social housing. She co-authored the *Ley de Fomento al Reciclaje* (Recycling Promotion Law), which was enacted in 2016, and was a vocal advocate for the rights of temporary agricultural workers, many of whom were Indigenous. Her legislative work also included efforts to reform Chile’s pension system, which she criticized for disproportionately affecting women and low-income workers.

Miranda’s political career faced setbacks in the mid-2010s. In 2013, she ran for re-election to the Chamber of Deputies but lost, securing only 12.1% of the vote. Undeterred, she remained active in politics, serving as the president of the Communist Party’s Santiago chapter from 2014 to 2016. In 2017, she ran for the Senate, representing the Santiago Metropolitan Region, but was unsuccessful, finishing fifth with 5.8% of the vote. Despite these losses, she continued to advocate for social causes, particularly those affecting Indigenous communities and women.

In her later years, Miranda shifted her focus to academia and activism. In 2018, she began teaching at the Universidad Academia de Humanismo Cristiano in Santiago, where she lectured on social policy and Indigenous rights. She also became a frequent commentator on political and social issues in Chilean media, contributing to outlets such as *El Mostrador* and *Radio Universidad de Chile*. In 2020, she was appointed as an advisor to the Ministry of Social Development under President Sebastián Piñera, where she worked on programs aimed at reducing poverty in Indigenous communities. However, she resigned from the position in 2021, citing disagreements with the government’s approach to social welfare.

Miranda has received several awards for her contributions to social justice. In 2012, she was honored with the *Premio Elena Caffarena* by the Chilean Network of Women in Management, recognizing her leadership in promoting gender equality. In 2015, the Mapuche organization *Ad Mapu* awarded her the *Premio Kimün* for her work in advancing Indigenous rights. Despite her political setbacks, she remains a prominent figure in Chilean leftist and Indigenous activism.

As of 2024, Roxana Miranda resides in Santiago, where she continues to write and speak on social issues. She is married to Luis González, a fellow social worker, and has two children, José and María. Her legacy is defined by her relentless advocacy for marginalized communities, her role as a trailblazer for Indigenous women in Chilean politics, and her contributions to social policy reform.

title: Diego Godín
text:
Diego Roberto Godín Leal was born on February 16, 1986, in Rosario, Uruguay, a city known for producing football talent. From a young age, Godín showed a passion for the sport, playing in local youth teams before joining Defensor Sporting’s academy in Montevideo at the age of 15. His early years were marked by determination, as he moved away from his family to pursue his dream. Defensor Sporting, a club with a strong youth development system, provided the foundation for his defensive skills, and he made his professional debut for the team on September 26, 2003, at the age of 17, in a Uruguayan Primera División match against Fénix.

Godín’s performances at Defensor Sporting earned him a move to Primera División side Nacional in 2006. During his single season with the club, he played 26 league matches and helped the team win the 2005-06 Uruguayan championship. His composed defending and leadership qualities caught the attention of European scouts, leading to a transfer to Villarreal CF in Spain’s La Liga in August 2007. The deal was reportedly worth €8 million, a significant sum for a young defender at the time. At Villarreal, Godín formed a strong partnership with Argentine defender Gonzalo Rodríguez, becoming a key figure in the team’s defense. Over three seasons, he made 116 appearances for the club, scoring 6 goals, and helped Villarreal secure a second-place finish in La Liga during the 2007-08 season, their highest-ever league position.

In August 2010, Godín joined Atlético Madrid for a reported fee of €8 million, signing a five-year contract. His arrival marked the beginning of a highly successful chapter in his career. Under manager Diego Simeone, who took charge in December 2011, Godín became a cornerstone of Atlético’s defense, known for his physicality, aerial ability, and tactical intelligence. One of his most memorable moments came on May 17, 2014, when he scored the decisive goal in the 116th minute of the UEFA Champions League final against Real Madrid at the Estádio da Luz in Lisbon. The 1-1 draw forced extra time, though Atlético eventually lost 4-1, but Godín’s header had already secured his place in the club’s history. That same season, Atlético won La Liga, ending a 18-year wait for the title, with Godín playing every minute of the league campaign. He also helped the team win the 2012 UEFA Europa League, the 2012 UEFA Super Cup, the 2013 Copa del Rey, and the 2018 UEFA Europa League, making him one of the most decorated defenders in the club’s history.

Internationally, Godín represented Uruguay from 2005 to 2022, earning 139 caps and scoring 8 goals, making him the second-most capped player in the country’s history behind goalkeeper Fernando Muslera. He made his debut on October 26, 2005, in a World Cup qualifier against Mexico. Godín was a key figure in Uruguay’s golden generation, playing in four FIFA World Cups (2010, 2014, 2018, and 2022) and five Copa América tournaments (2007, 2011, 2015, 2016, and 2019). His leadership was instrumental in Uruguay’s victory at the 2011 Copa América, where they won their 15th continental title. In the 2010 World Cup, he helped Uruguay reach the semifinals, their best finish since 1970, and in the 2018 World Cup, he captained the team to the quarterfinals. His final international appearance came on November 24, 2022, in a 2-0 loss to Portugal at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

After leaving Atlético Madrid in 2019, Godín’s career entered a new phase. He signed a three-year contract with Inter Milan, where he made 23 Serie A appearances in his first season, though his playing time diminished in his second year. In September 2020, he joined Cagliari on a free transfer, spending two seasons in Sardinia before moving to Atlético Mineiro in Brazil in January 2022. At Atlético Mineiro, he won the Campeonato Mineiro and the Copa do Brasil in 2022, adding to his already impressive trophy collection. In January 2023, he returned to Argentina to join Vélez Sarsfield, where he played 12 matches before announcing his retirement from professional football on July 27, 2023, at the age of 37.

Beyond football, Godín has been involved in charitable work, particularly in Uruguay, where he has supported initiatives for underprivileged children. He is married to Sofía Herrera, and the couple has two children. Known for his professionalism and humility, Godín remains one of the most respected defenders of his generation, celebrated for his consistency, leadership, and ability to perform in high-pressure situations. His career, spanning nearly two decades, saw him play over 700 professional matches and win numerous domestic and international titles, cementing his legacy as one of Uruguay’s greatest footballers.

title: Lunay (singer)
text:
Jefnier Osorio Moreno, known professionally as Lunay, is a Puerto Rican reggaeton and Latin trap singer and songwriter. Born on October 4, 2000, in Corozal, Puerto Rico, Lunay grew up in a musically inclined family. His father, José Osorio, was a musician, and his mother, Jennifer Moreno, was a singer, which exposed him to music from an early age. Lunay’s interest in music was further fueled by his exposure to reggaeton and Latin trap, genres that were gaining popularity in Puerto Rico during his childhood.

Lunay’s musical journey began in his teenage years when he started posting covers of popular songs on social media platforms like Instagram and YouTube. His talent quickly caught the attention of listeners, and his following grew rapidly. By 2017, he had gained a significant online presence, which led to collaborations with established artists in the Latin music scene. One of his earliest breakthroughs came when he was featured on the song *"A Solas"* by Lyanno, Bryant Myers, and Alex Rose, released in November 2017. The track became a hit, garnering millions of streams and establishing Lunay as a rising star.

In 2018, Lunay signed a record deal with Star Island Music, a subsidiary of Universal Music Latin Entertainment. This partnership marked a turning point in his career, providing him with the resources and platform to release his own music. His debut single, *"Aventura"*, was released on May 25, 2018, and became an instant success, amassing over 100 million views on YouTube within a few months. The song’s catchy melody and Lunay’s distinctive voice resonated with audiences, solidifying his place in the reggaeton scene.

Lunay’s rise to fame continued with the release of his second single, *"Luz Apaga"*, on October 19, 2018. The track, which featured Darell, Ozuna, and Lyanno, became another major hit, further expanding his fanbase. The song’s success was followed by the release of his debut EP, *"Épico"*, on November 23, 2018. The EP included six tracks, including collaborations with artists like Anuel AA, Noriel, and Alex Rose, and showcased Lunay’s versatility as an artist. *"Épico"* debuted at number 12 on the *Billboard* Latin Rhythm Albums chart and received critical acclaim for its blend of reggaeton, trap, and melodic influences.

In 2019, Lunay continued to build on his momentum with the release of several successful singles, including *"Soltera"* featuring Daddy Yankee and Bad Bunny, which was released on May 10, 2019. The song became a global hit, peaking at number 13 on the *Billboard* Hot Latin Songs chart and earning Lunay his first *Billboard* Latin Music Award nomination for Hot Latin Song of the Year. The track’s success was followed by *"La Cama"*, a collaboration with Myke Towers, which was released on July 19, 2019, and also became a commercial success.

Lunay’s debut studio album, *"Épico"*, was released on October 25, 2019, and included 14 tracks, featuring collaborations with artists like Wisin & Yandel, Zion & Lennox, and Rauw Alejandro. The album debuted at number 22 on the *Billboard* Top Latin Albums chart and received positive reviews for its energetic production and Lunay’s vocal performance. The album’s lead single, *"Aventura (Remix)"*, featuring Anuel AA and Ozuna, became a massive hit, further cementing Lunay’s status as one of reggaeton’s most promising young artists.

Throughout 2020 and 2021, Lunay continued to release new music, including collaborations with artists like Sech, Justin Quiles, and Chencho Corleone. His single *"Relación"*, released on September 4, 2020, became one of his biggest hits, peaking at number 6 on the *Billboard* Hot Latin Songs chart and earning a Latin Grammy nomination for Best Urban Song. The song’s success was followed by *"La Cama (Remix)"*, featuring Myke Towers, Rauw Alejandro, and Ozuna, which was released on December 4, 2020, and became another commercial success.

In addition to his musical achievements, Lunay has also ventured into entrepreneurship. In 2021, he launched his own record label, *Lunay Music Group*, in partnership with Universal Music Latin Entertainment. The label aims to support and develop new talent in the Latin music industry. Lunay has also been involved in philanthropic efforts, including donations to communities in Puerto Rico affected by natural disasters.

As of 2024, Lunay continues to be a prominent figure in the Latin music industry, known for his energetic performances and catchy songs. His music has amassed billions of streams across platforms, and he has collaborated with some of the biggest names in reggaeton and Latin trap. Despite his young age, Lunay has already achieved significant success and shows no signs of slowing down, with new projects and collaborations on the horizon. His journey from a small-town artist in Puerto Rico to an international star serves as an inspiration to aspiring musicians worldwide.

title: Trevor Noah
text:
Trevor Noah was born on February 20, 1984, in Johannesburg, South Africa, during the final decade of apartheid, a system of institutionalized racial segregation. His mother, Patricia Nombuyiselo Noah, was a Black Xhosa woman, and his father, Robert Noah, was a white Swiss-German man. Under apartheid laws, their relationship was illegal, and Trevor’s birth was a criminal act. His mother, a devout Christian, raised him primarily in the township of Soweto, a historically Black urban area, while his father remained largely absent due to the legal risks. Patricia worked as a typist and later as a secretary, instilling in Trevor a strong work ethic and a love for education. She often took him to church, where he developed an early appreciation for storytelling and performance.

Noah’s childhood was marked by poverty and the harsh realities of apartheid’s aftermath. He attended Maryvale College, a Catholic school in Johannesburg, where he was one of the few mixed-race students. Despite facing bullying and social exclusion, he excelled academically and developed a sharp wit, using humor as a coping mechanism. After high school, he briefly studied at the University of South Africa but dropped out to pursue a career in entertainment. In his late teens, he began performing as a DJ under the name "DJ Edu," spinning records at local parties and clubs in Johannesburg. By 2002, he had transitioned into stand-up comedy, performing at small venues like the Pivot in Johannesburg’s Newtown district.

Noah’s breakthrough came in 2009 when he won the South African Comedy Award for Best Newcomer. His sharp, observational humor, often centered on race, identity, and South African culture, quickly gained attention. In 2010, he performed at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, his first major international appearance, where he was praised for his unique perspective as a biracial comedian from post-apartheid South Africa. That same year, he released his first stand-up special, *The Daywalker*, which showcased his ability to blend personal anecdotes with social commentary. By 2012, he had performed on *The Tonight Show with Jay Leno* and *The Late Show with David Letterman*, becoming one of the first South African comedians to achieve mainstream recognition in the U.S.

In 2013, Noah released his second stand-up special, *That’s Racist*, and published his memoir, *Born a Crime: Stories from a South African Childhood*, which detailed his upbringing under apartheid. The book became a *New York Times* bestseller, spending over two years on the list and selling over three million copies worldwide. Its success cemented Noah’s reputation as a compelling storyteller beyond comedy. In 2014, he joined *The Daily Show* as a contributor, and in September 2015, following Jon Stewart’s departure, he was named the show’s new host. At 31, he became the first South African to anchor a major American late-night program. Under his leadership, *The Daily Show* won multiple Emmy Awards, including Outstanding Variety Talk Series in 2017, 2018, and 2021. His tenure also saw the show’s digital presence expand, with segments like *Between the Scenes* and *The Daily Show: Ears Edition* podcast reaching millions of viewers.

Beyond comedy, Noah became a prominent voice on social and political issues. In 2017, he founded the Trevor Noah Foundation, a nonprofit aimed at improving educational opportunities for South African youth. The foundation partnered with organizations like the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation to provide scholarships and resources to underprivileged students. In 2018, he hosted the Grammy Awards, further solidifying his status as a global entertainer. That same year, he released his third stand-up special, *Son of Patricia*, which premiered on Netflix and received critical acclaim. In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, he launched *The Daily Social Distancing Show*, a reimagined version of *The Daily Show* that addressed the crisis with his signature humor and insight.

Noah’s personal life has been relatively private, though he has been open about his relationships. From 2014 to 2018, he dated model and entrepreneur Jordyn Taylor. In 2022, he announced his departure from *The Daily Show*, delivering his final episode on December 8 of that year after seven years as host. He cited a desire to focus on his stand-up career and other creative projects. In 2023, he released *I Wish You Would*, his fourth Netflix special, which reflected on his experiences as a global figure and the challenges of fame. As of 2024, Noah continues to tour internationally, perform stand-up, and work on various media projects, including a potential film adaptation of *Born a Crime*. His influence as a comedian, commentator, and advocate for social justice remains significant, with a net worth estimated at over $100 million.

title: Adel Emam
text:
Adel Emam, born on May 17, 1940, in Mansoura, Egypt, is one of the most celebrated actors in the Arab world, renowned for his contributions to Egyptian cinema, theater, and television. His full name is Adel Mohamed Emam, and he grew up in a middle-class family in the Shubra district of Cairo, where his father worked as a government employee. From an early age, Emam displayed a keen interest in acting, inspired by the vibrant theater scene in Egypt during the 1950s. He attended Ain Shams University, where he studied agriculture, but his passion for performance led him to join the university’s theater group, laying the foundation for his future career.

Emam’s professional acting debut came in 1962 when he appeared in the play *"Al-Nas Elli Taht"* (The People Downstairs) at the Comedy Theater in Cairo. His early roles were minor, but his talent for comedy and timing quickly set him apart. By the mid-1960s, he had transitioned to film, making his cinematic debut in *"Ana wa Huwa wa Hiya"* (Me, Him, and Her, 1964), directed by Fatin Abdel Wahab. Though his role was small, it marked the beginning of a prolific career that would span over six decades. Throughout the 1960s and 1970s, Emam appeared in numerous films, often in supporting roles, gradually building his reputation as a versatile actor. Some of his notable early works include *"Al-Irhabi"* (The Terrorist, 1965) and *"Al-Zawja al-Thaniya"* (The Second Wife, 1967).

The 1980s and 1990s were the golden years of Adel Emam’s career, during which he became a household name across the Arab world. He starred in a series of commercially successful and critically acclaimed films that cemented his status as Egypt’s leading comedic and dramatic actor. In 1980, he delivered a breakthrough performance in *"Al-Irhab wal-Kabab"* (Terrorism and Kebab), a satirical comedy directed by Sherif Arafa that tackled bureaucratic corruption in Egypt. The film was a massive hit, grossing over 1.5 million Egyptian pounds (a significant sum at the time) and becoming one of the highest-grossing Egyptian films of the decade. Emam’s portrayal of a frustrated citizen who accidentally takes hostages in a government building showcased his ability to blend humor with social commentary, a hallmark of his later work.

Another defining role came in 1984 with *"Al-Avokato"* (The Lawyer), directed by Atef El-Tayeb, where Emam played a morally ambiguous lawyer navigating the complexities of Egypt’s legal system. The film was a critical success and earned him widespread praise for his dramatic depth. Throughout the 1980s, Emam collaborated frequently with director Sherif Arafa, producing hits like *"Al-Mushaghibun"* (The Troublemakers, 1988) and *"Al-Irhabi"* (The Terrorist, 1994), the latter of which was Egypt’s official submission for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. His ability to shift between comedy and drama made him a unique figure in Arab cinema, and by the 1990s, he had become one of the highest-paid actors in the region, commanding fees of up to 1 million Egyptian pounds per film.

Emam’s career extended beyond cinema into television, where he starred in several successful series. In 1992, he appeared in *"Lan Aishi fi Gilbab Abi"* (I Won’t Live in My Father’s Robe), a drama series that explored generational conflicts in Egyptian society. The show was a ratings success and further expanded his fan base. He also ventured into theater, starring in productions like *"School of Mischief"* (1995), which ran for over 300 performances in Cairo and other Arab cities. His stage work demonstrated his versatility, as he often performed in both classical and contemporary plays.

Despite his success, Emam’s career was not without controversy. In 2012, he faced legal challenges when he was sentenced *in absentia* to three months in prison for "defaming Islam" in some of his films, including *"Al-Irhabi"* (1994) and *"Morgan Ahmed Morgan"* (2007). The case, brought by conservative lawyers, sparked debates about freedom of expression in Egypt. Emam, who had been living abroad at the time, denied the charges, and the sentence was later overturned on appeal. The incident highlighted the political and social tensions in Egypt during the post-revolutionary period, but it did little to diminish his popularity.

In his later years, Emam continued to act but at a reduced pace. He starred in *"Hassan wa Morcus"* (2016), a comedy-drama directed by Rami Imam, his son, which was well-received by audiences. The film marked a rare father-son collaboration and demonstrated Emam’s enduring appeal. As of 2024, he remains a cultural icon, with a filmography that includes over 100 films, 20 television series, and numerous theater productions. His contributions to Egyptian and Arab cinema have earned him numerous awards, including the Lifetime Achievement Award at the Cairo International Film Festival in 2005 and the Dubai International Film Festival in 2010.

Adel Emam’s personal life has been relatively private. He married twice; his first marriage was to Hala al-Shalakani, with whom he had three children: Rami, Sarah, and Mohamed. His son Rami Imam is a prominent film director and producer. Emam’s second marriage was to actress Nahla Fathi, though the couple later divorced. Despite his fame, he has maintained a low public profile, focusing on his work and family. Now in his eighties, Emam remains a beloved figure in the Arab world, celebrated for his ability to entertain while addressing social and political issues through his art. His legacy as one of Egypt’s greatest actors is firmly secured, with his films continuing to resonate with audiences across generations.

title: Mattias Asper
text:
Mattias Asper was born on March 20, 1974, in Sölvesborg, a small town in Blekinge County, Sweden. From an early age, he displayed a strong passion for football, a sport deeply embedded in Swedish culture. Asper began his youth career at local club Sölvesborgs GoIF, where his talent as a goalkeeper quickly became evident. His performances at the youth level caught the attention of larger clubs, and in 1993, at the age of 19, he signed his first professional contract with Mjällby AIF, a club based in Hällevik, also in Blekinge County.

Asper’s professional debut came in 1993 during Mjällby’s campaign in Division 1, Sweden’s second-tier league at the time. His agility, reflexes, and command of the penalty area made him a standout player, and by 1995, he had established himself as the team’s first-choice goalkeeper. That same year, Mjällby secured promotion to the Allsvenskan, Sweden’s top division, marking a significant milestone in both the club’s and Asper’s careers. However, the team struggled in the top flight, and after one season, they were relegated back to Division 1.

In 1997, Asper made a pivotal move to AIK Fotboll, one of Sweden’s most prestigious clubs, based in Stockholm. His transfer was a turning point, as AIK was competing in the Allsvenskan and had ambitions to challenge for domestic and European honors. Asper quickly became the team’s starting goalkeeper, making his debut on April 14, 1997, in a 2-0 victory over Örebro SK. That season, AIK finished second in the league, and Asper’s performances earned him widespread recognition. The following year, 1998, was even more successful. AIK won the Allsvenskan title, finishing three points ahead of Helsingborgs IF, with Asper playing a crucial role in the team’s defense. He also helped AIK secure the Svenska Cupen (Swedish Cup) that year, completing a domestic double.

Asper’s success at AIK attracted interest from abroad, and in 1999, he signed with Real Sociedad, a La Liga club based in San Sebastián, Spain. His time in Spain was challenging, as he struggled to secure a starting position behind established goalkeeper Alberto López. Asper made only 11 league appearances for Real Sociedad over two seasons, from 1999 to 2001, before returning to Sweden. In 2001, he joined Malmö FF, another of Sweden’s top clubs, where he regained his form. Over the next four seasons, Asper became a key figure in Malmö’s defense, making over 100 appearances for the club. In 2004, he played a vital role in Malmö’s Allsvenskan title win, their first in 16 years, and was named the league’s best goalkeeper that season.

After leaving Malmö in 2005, Asper had a brief stint with Viking FK in Norway’s Tippeligaen, where he made 14 league appearances. He then returned to Sweden, signing with IFK Norrköping in 2006. His time at Norrköping was less successful, as the club struggled in the Allsvenskan, and Asper faced competition for the starting role. In 2008, he moved to his hometown club, Mjällby AIF, which had recently been promoted to the Allsvenskan. Asper played a crucial role in helping the club establish itself in the top division, making 55 league appearances over three seasons. His leadership and experience were invaluable, and he became a fan favorite.

Asper retired from professional football in 2011 at the age of 37. Over his career, he made a total of 324 appearances in the Allsvenskan, placing him among the league’s most experienced goalkeepers. He also earned three caps for the Swedish national team, making his debut on February 24, 2001, in a friendly match against Thailand. Though his international career was limited, his club achievements solidified his reputation as one of Sweden’s most reliable goalkeepers of his generation.

After retiring, Asper remained involved in football, working as a goalkeeper coach and occasionally as a commentator for Swedish football broadcasts. He also pursued business interests, including a brief role as a partner in a sports management company. In his personal life, Asper has kept a relatively low profile, residing in southern Sweden with his family. His contributions to Swedish football, particularly his success with AIK and Malmö FF, have left a lasting legacy in the sport.

title: G. Fowler Stewart
text:
G. Fowler Stewart was born George Fowler Stewart on March 12, 1878, in Edinburgh, Scotland, to George Stewart, a merchant, and Margaret Fowler Stewart. He was the eldest of four children, with two brothers, William and James, and a sister, Elizabeth. The family lived in a modest but comfortable home at 12 Bruntsfield Place, a respectable neighborhood in the southern part of the city. Stewart attended the prestigious Edinburgh Academy, where he excelled in mathematics and science, graduating in 1896 with top honors in his class.

After completing his secondary education, Stewart enrolled at the University of Edinburgh to study engineering. He earned his Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering in 1900, ranking first in his cohort of 47 students. His academic performance earned him a scholarship to pursue postgraduate studies at the University of Glasgow, where he specialized in structural engineering. In 1902, he completed his Master of Science degree, submitting a thesis on the design of steel bridges, which was later published in the *Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers* in 1903.

Stewart’s professional career began in 1903 when he joined the engineering firm of Sir John Wolfe Barry & Partners in London. Wolfe Barry, a renowned civil engineer best known for designing London’s Tower Bridge, took Stewart under his wing. Stewart worked on several high-profile projects, including the expansion of the Port of London and the construction of the Blackwall Tunnel. His meticulous calculations and innovative approaches to load distribution earned him recognition within the firm, and by 1907, he was promoted to senior engineer.

In 1910, Stewart left Wolfe Barry’s firm to establish his own consultancy, Stewart & Associates, based in Westminster. The firm quickly gained a reputation for its expertise in bridge design and structural analysis. One of Stewart’s earliest major commissions was the design of the Forth Road Bridge in Scotland, a project that began in 1912. Although construction was delayed by World War I, Stewart’s preliminary designs laid the groundwork for the bridge’s eventual completion in 1964. During the war, Stewart served as a lieutenant in the Royal Engineers, where he applied his engineering skills to the construction of temporary bridges and fortifications. He was awarded the Military Cross in 1917 for his work in designing a pontoon bridge under enemy fire near Ypres, Belgium.

After the war, Stewart returned to his consultancy and expanded its operations. In 1922, he was appointed as the chief consulting engineer for the Sydney Harbour Bridge project in Australia. His firm was responsible for the structural calculations and stress analysis of the bridge’s iconic arch design. Construction began in 1923, and Stewart made several trips to Australia to oversee the project, which was completed in 1932. The bridge, with a main span of 503 meters, was the world’s widest long-span bridge at the time and remains one of Australia’s most recognizable landmarks.

Stewart’s career flourished in the 1930s, as he took on increasingly complex projects. In 1935, he was commissioned to design the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco, though his involvement was later scaled back due to disagreements with the project’s chief engineer, Joseph Strauss. Nevertheless, Stewart’s firm contributed to the bridge’s structural analysis, particularly in addressing wind resistance and seismic stability. The Golden Gate Bridge opened in 1937, with a main span of 1,280 meters, making it the longest suspension bridge in the world at the time.

In his later years, Stewart shifted his focus to education and advocacy for engineering standards. In 1940, he was elected president of the Institution of Civil Engineers, a position he held until 1942. During his tenure, he pushed for the adoption of uniform safety codes in bridge construction, which were later incorporated into British engineering regulations. He also served as a visiting lecturer at Imperial College London, where he mentored a generation of engineers.

Stewart retired in 1948 at the age of 70, though he remained active as a consultant for several years. He published his memoirs, *Bridges and Beyond*, in 1952, which detailed his experiences on major projects and offered insights into the evolution of structural engineering. Stewart married Margaret MacLeod in 1905, and the couple had three children: George Jr., born in 1906; Eleanor, born in 1908; and Robert, born in 1912. Margaret passed away in 1955, and Stewart lived quietly in his later years at his home in Surrey. He died on November 3, 1962, at the age of 84, following a brief illness. He was buried in the family plot at Dean Cemetery in Edinburgh, leaving behind a legacy as one of the most influential civil engineers of the early 20th century.

title: Sérgio Moraes
text:
Sérgio Moraes, born on October 23, 1982, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, is a retired mixed martial artist and Brazilian jiu-jitsu practitioner who competed in the welterweight division of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC). Moraes grew up in the working-class neighborhood of Vila Isabel, where he was introduced to martial arts at an early age. His father, a former amateur boxer, encouraged him to train in combat sports, and by the age of 12, Moraes began practicing judo at a local dojo. His interest in grappling deepened when he transitioned to Brazilian jiu-jitsu (BJJ) at 16, training under the guidance of Carlos Machado, a prominent figure in the sport.

Moraes quickly distinguished himself in BJJ, earning his black belt in 2006 under Machado’s tutelage. His competitive career in BJJ was marked by several notable achievements, including a gold medal at the 2005 World Jiu-Jitsu Championship in the brown belt middleweight division. He also secured victories in the Brazilian National Championships and the Pan Jiu-Jitsu Championship, establishing himself as a formidable grappler before transitioning to mixed martial arts (MMA).

Moraes made his professional MMA debut on March 1, 2008, at the *Bitetti Combat 2* event in Rio de Janeiro, where he defeated Thiago Santos by submission (rear-naked choke) in the first round. Over the next two years, he amassed a record of 6-0, with five of his six wins coming by submission, showcasing his elite grappling skills. His undefeated streak earned him an invitation to compete on *The Ultimate Fighter: Brazil* (TUF Brazil), a reality television series produced by the UFC, which aired in 2012.

On *TUF Brazil*, Moraes was coached by former UFC middleweight champion Vitor Belfort and competed in the welterweight division. He won his preliminary bout against Thiago Perpétuo by submission (rear-naked choke) and advanced to the quarterfinals, where he defeated Renée Forte by unanimous decision. In the semifinals, he faced Delson Heleno, winning by submission (arm-triangle choke) in the first round. Moraes went on to win the tournament final against Thiago Perpétuo at *UFC 147* on June 23, 2012, securing a split decision victory and earning a UFC contract.

Following his *TUF Brazil* victory, Moraes made his official UFC debut at *UFC 153* on October 13, 2012, in Rio de Janeiro, where he faced fellow TUF Brazil alumnus Renee Forte. Moraes won the fight by submission (rear-naked choke) in the third round. His next bout came at *UFC on Fuel TV 10* on June 8, 2013, against Neil Magny, which he lost by unanimous decision, marking his first defeat in the UFC. Despite the setback, Moraes rebounded with a submission win over Zak Cummings at *UFC Fight Night 38* on March 23, 2014, earning a *Performance of the Night* bonus.

Moraes continued to compete in the UFC for several years, facing notable opponents such as Peter Sobotta, Omari Akhmedov, and Kamaru Usman. His most significant victory came at *UFC Fight Night 95* on September 24, 2016, when he knocked out Luan Chagas in the third round, earning another *Performance of the Night* award. Over his UFC career, Moraes compiled a record of 14-6-1 (1 NC), with seven of his wins coming by submission and two by knockout.

Outside of the UFC, Moraes also competed in other promotions, including a brief stint in the Russian-based Absolute Championship Berkut (ACB), where he faced Albert Duraev in 2018. After leaving the UFC in 2020, Moraes transitioned to coaching and commentary, working with younger fighters in Brazil and providing analysis for MMA events. He officially announced his retirement from professional competition in 2021, ending a career that spanned over a decade.

In his later years, Moraes remained active in the martial arts community, opening his own gym, *Equipe Moraes*, in Rio de Janeiro, where he taught Brazilian jiu-jitsu and MMA. He also became a regular contributor to MMA media, offering insights on grappling and fight strategy. Despite never capturing a UFC title, Moraes is remembered for his technical prowess, resilience, and contributions to the sport, particularly in his native Brazil. As of 2024, he continues to reside in Rio de Janeiro, where he focuses on coaching and mentoring the next generation of fighters.

title: Abdullahi Mohammad Ahmad Hassan
text:
Abdullahi Mohammad Ahmad Hassan, often referred to as Abdullahi Mohammad or simply Abdullahi Hassan, was a prominent Somali military officer, politician, and diplomat whose career spanned several decades of Somalia’s turbulent post-independence history. Born on January 1, 1939, in the town of Beledweyne, situated in the Hiiraan region of central Somalia, he grew up during a period of colonial rule under Italian administration. His early education took place in local schools before he pursued further studies in Mogadishu, where he attended the prestigious Scuola Militare di Mogadiscio, a military academy established by the Italians to train Somali officers.

Hassan’s military career began in earnest in the early 1960s, following Somalia’s independence from Italy on July 1, 1960. He was among the first generation of Somali officers trained in both Italian and later Soviet military institutions, reflecting the shifting geopolitical alliances of the Cold War era. By 1963, he had risen through the ranks of the Somali National Army (SNA), which was then a fledgling institution tasked with consolidating the newly unified territories of former British Somaliland and Italian Somalia. His early postings included roles in infantry units, where he gained a reputation for discipline and strategic acumen.

In 1969, Hassan’s career took a dramatic turn when General Mohamed Siad Barre led a bloodless coup d’état on October 21, overthrowing the civilian government of President Abdirashid Ali Shermarke, who had been assassinated earlier that month. Hassan, then a lieutenant colonel, aligned himself with the new military regime, which established the Supreme Revolutionary Council (SRC) to govern Somalia. Under Siad Barre’s socialist-oriented government, Hassan was appointed to several key positions, including Director of Military Intelligence (1970–1974), where he played a crucial role in consolidating the regime’s control over the military and security apparatus. During this period, he was instrumental in suppressing dissent and overseeing the integration of former colonial military structures into a unified national force.

One of Hassan’s most notable achievements came during the Ogaden War (1977–1978), a conflict between Somalia and Ethiopia over the disputed Ogaden region. As a brigadier general, he commanded the 21st Division of the Somali National Army, which spearheaded the initial offensive into Ethiopian territory. The Somali forces achieved significant early victories, capturing the strategic towns of Jijiga and Dire Dawa by September 1977. However, the tide turned when the Soviet Union, which had previously supported Somalia, switched allegiance to Ethiopia, providing massive military aid and Cuban combat troops. By March 1978, Somali forces were forced into a humiliating retreat, marking a turning point in Hassan’s military career. Despite the defeat, his leadership during the war earned him both praise and criticism, with some regarding him as a capable commander while others blamed him for the strategic miscalculations that led to Somalia’s eventual loss.

Following the Ogaden War, Hassan transitioned into diplomatic and political roles. In 1980, he was appointed Somalia’s Ambassador to the Soviet Union, a position he held until 1984. This appointment was part of Siad Barre’s efforts to mend relations with the USSR after the rupture caused by the Ogaden conflict. During his tenure in Moscow, Hassan worked to secure limited military and economic assistance, though Somalia’s relationship with the Soviet Union never fully recovered to its pre-war levels. Upon his return to Somalia, he was reassigned to domestic roles, including Minister of Defense (1984–1986) and later Minister of the Interior (1986–1988). In these capacities, he oversaw the increasingly repressive measures of Siad Barre’s regime, which by the late 1980s was facing growing armed resistance from clan-based militias, particularly in the north.

Hassan’s later years were marked by the collapse of Siad Barre’s government in January 1991, following years of civil war and economic decline. Unlike many of his contemporaries, he managed to avoid the violent purges and clan-based retributions that followed the regime’s fall. He went into exile, first in Kenya and later in Italy, where he lived quietly for several years. In the mid-1990s, he briefly returned to Somalia during the early attempts at national reconciliation, including the 1993 Addis Ababa peace talks, but his involvement in post-war politics was limited. He spent his final years in Rome, where he passed away on November 15, 2012, at the age of 73. His death was largely unnoticed by the international media, reflecting the obscurity into which many of Somalia’s once-powerful figures had fallen in the aftermath of the state’s collapse. Despite the controversies surrounding his career, Abdullahi Mohammad Ahmad Hassan remains a significant figure in Somalia’s military and political history, embodying the complexities of a nation torn between ambition, ideology, and internal strife.

title: Rosé (singer)
text:
Roseanne Park, known professionally as Rosé, was born on February 11, 1997, in Auckland, New Zealand, to South Korean immigrant parents. Her family moved to Melbourne, Australia, when she was seven years old, and she grew up in the suburb of Box Hill. Rosé attended Canterbury Girls' Secondary College, where she was an active student, participating in choir and learning to play the guitar and piano. Her early exposure to music came from her father, who enjoyed listening to artists like Eric Clapton and The Beatles, while her mother introduced her to K-pop, sparking her interest in the genre.

Rosé’s journey to becoming a global K-pop star began in 2012 when she auditioned for YG Entertainment, one of South Korea’s most prominent entertainment companies, during their Australian auditions. She sang "I Will Always Love You" by Whitney Houston and impressed the judges, earning a spot as a trainee. She moved to Seoul later that year, at the age of 15, to begin her rigorous training. Her time as a trainee lasted four years, during which she honed her vocal skills, dance abilities, and stage presence alongside other trainees who would later debut in various YG groups.

On August 8, 2016, Rosé made her official debut as the main vocalist of the girl group BLACKPINK, alongside members Jisoo, Jennie, and Lisa. The group’s debut single album, *Square One*, featured the tracks "Boombayah" and "Whistle," both of which achieved immediate success. "Whistle" topped the Gaon Digital Chart, making BLACKPINK the fastest group to achieve a number-one hit on the chart since their debut. Rosé’s powerful vocals and charismatic stage presence quickly made her a standout member, earning her a dedicated fanbase.

BLACKPINK’s rise to international fame was swift. In 2018, the group released their first extended play, *Square Up*, which included the hit single "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du." The song peaked at number 55 on the *Billboard* Hot 100, making BLACKPINK the first K-pop girl group to enter the chart. Rosé’s solo performances, such as her cover of "Coming Home" by Diddy-Dirty Money during BLACKPINK’s 2019 Coachella performance, further showcased her vocal range and versatility. That same year, BLACKPINK became the first K-pop girl group to perform at Coachella, solidifying their status as global icons.

Rosé’s solo career began to take shape in 2020 when YG Entertainment announced that each BLACKPINK member would release solo projects. On March 12, 2021, she debuted as a solo artist with the single album *-R-*, which included the title track "On the Ground" and the B-side "Gone." "On the Ground" debuted at number 70 on the *Billboard* Hot 100, making Rosé the first female K-pop soloist to enter the chart. The song also topped the *Billboard* Global 200, making her the first Korean solo artist to achieve this feat. The music video for "On the Ground" broke records, amassing 41.6 million views in its first 24 hours, the most for a solo K-pop artist at the time. The album itself sold over 400,000 copies in its first week, setting a new record for a female K-pop soloist.

Beyond music, Rosé has ventured into fashion and philanthropy. She was appointed as a global ambassador for Yves Saint Laurent in 2020, becoming the first K-pop idol to represent the brand. She has also collaborated with brands like Tiffany & Co. and has been featured in magazines such as *Vogue* and *Elle*. In 2021, she donated 100 million KRW (approximately $85,000 USD) to the Hope Bridge Korea Disaster Relief Association to support victims of wildfires in South Korea.

As of 2024, Rosé continues to be an active member of BLACKPINK, which has achieved numerous milestones, including headlining Coachella in 2023 and embarking on the *Born Pink World Tour*, one of the highest-grossing tours by a female act. She remains a prominent figure in K-pop, known for her vocal talent, fashion influence, and global appeal. Despite her fame, she has maintained a relatively private personal life, focusing on her career and creative endeavors. Her journey from a young girl in Melbourne to a global superstar serves as an inspiration to aspiring artists worldwide.

title: Billy Conigliaro
text:
Billy Conigliaro was born William Michael Conigliaro on August 15, 1947, in Revere, Massachusetts, a working-class city just north of Boston. He was the younger brother of Tony Conigliaro, who would later become a star outfielder for the Boston Red Sox. Growing up in a baseball-loving family, Billy was immersed in the sport from an early age, often playing alongside his brother in local leagues. His father, Sal Conigliaro, a former semipro player, and his mother, Teresa, encouraged both boys to pursue their athletic dreams. Billy attended Revere High School, where he excelled as a multi-sport athlete, particularly in baseball and basketball. His powerful arm and natural hitting ability made him a standout, and by his senior year in 1965, he was already drawing attention from Major League scouts.

The Boston Red Sox selected Billy Conigliaro in the first round (fifth overall) of the 1965 Major League Baseball Amateur Draft, the same year his brother Tony made his MLB debut. Unlike Tony, who had skipped the minor leagues, Billy was sent to the Red Sox’s farm system to develop. He spent the 1965 season with the Waterloo Hawks in the Class A Midwest League, where he batted .282 with 11 home runs and 55 RBIs in 118 games. The following year, he was promoted to the Pittsfield Red Sox of the Double-A Eastern League, where he improved his numbers, hitting .293 with 15 home runs and 62 RBIs in 130 games. His performance earned him a late-season call-up to the Triple-A Toronto Maple Leafs in 1967, though he played only a handful of games before the season ended.

Billy made his Major League debut on September 10, 1969, at the age of 22, joining his brother Tony in the Red Sox outfield. He appeared in 17 games that season, batting .241 with two home runs and six RBIs. The following year, 1970, was his first full season in the majors, and he quickly established himself as a reliable hitter. Playing primarily as a left fielder, he batted .271 with 18 home runs and 58 RBIs in 114 games. His best statistical season came in 1971, when he hit .276 with 22 home runs and 74 RBIs, finishing 16th in the American League MVP voting. That year, he also set a career high with 156 hits and 28 doubles. The Conigliaro brothers, along with fellow outfielder Reggie Smith, formed one of the most formidable offensive outfields in baseball, drawing comparisons to the Red Sox’s legendary 1967 "Impossible Dream" team.

Despite his early success, Billy’s career was derailed by injuries and personal struggles. In 1972, he suffered a severe ankle injury in a collision with the outfield wall at Fenway Park on May 28, which limited him to just 60 games that season. He returned in 1973 but struggled to regain his form, batting only .222 with 11 home runs in 109 games. The Red Sox traded him to the Milwaukee Brewers on December 7, 1973, in a deal that sent him and George Scott to Milwaukee in exchange for Bernie Carbo and two other players. His time with the Brewers was short-lived; he played only 14 games in 1974 before being released on May 1. He briefly signed with the Oakland Athletics later that year but appeared in just 11 games before his MLB career came to an end.

After retiring from baseball, Billy Conigliaro struggled with personal demons, including alcoholism and financial difficulties. Unlike his brother Tony, who remained a beloved figure in Boston, Billy largely faded from public view. He worked odd jobs in the Boston area, including stints as a bartender and a construction worker. His life was further marked by tragedy when Tony suffered a devastating beaning in 1967 that nearly ended his career and later died in 1990 at the age of 45 due to complications from a stroke. Billy himself faced health issues in his later years, including heart problems. On February 10, 2021, he passed away at the age of 73 in Salem, New Hampshire, due to complications from a heart attack. Though his career was shorter and less celebrated than his brother’s, Billy Conigliaro remains a notable figure in Red Sox history, remembered for his power at the plate and the brief but exciting partnership he shared with Tony in Boston’s outfield.

title: Arif Mohammad Khan
text:
Arif Mohammad Khan was born on November 18, 1951, in Bulandshahr, Uttar Pradesh, India, into a Muslim family with a background in public service. His father, Mohammad Naseem Khan, was a freedom fighter and a member of the Indian National Congress, which influenced Khan’s early exposure to politics. He completed his schooling in Bulandshahr and later pursued a Bachelor of Arts degree from Aligarh Muslim University (AMU) in 1971. He went on to earn a Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) from the same institution in 1974, where he was actively involved in student politics and developed a keen interest in constitutional law and governance.

Khan’s political career began in the early 1970s when he joined the Indian National Congress (INC) as a student leader. His articulate oratory and commitment to secularism quickly brought him into the party’s mainstream. In 1977, at the age of 26, he contested and won his first election to the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Assembly from the Siana constituency in Bulandshahr, representing the Janata Party after the Congress split following the Emergency. However, his tenure was short-lived as the assembly was dissolved in 1979. He returned to the Congress in 1980 and was re-elected to the Uttar Pradesh Assembly from the same constituency, serving until 1984.

In 1984, Khan was elected to the Lok Sabha, the lower house of India’s Parliament, from the Kanpur constituency, securing 330,000 votes, a significant margin in a closely watched election. His tenure in Parliament was marked by his vocal stance on social and constitutional issues, particularly his opposition to religious conservatism. One of his most notable contributions came in 1986 during the debate on the Shah Bano case, a landmark legal battle involving Muslim personal law and maintenance rights for divorced women. Khan, then a Minister of State in the Rajiv Gandhi government, publicly supported the Supreme Court’s judgment, which granted Shah Bano the right to maintenance under Section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code. His stance put him at odds with conservative Muslim groups and even sections of his own party, leading to his resignation from the Congress on February 25, 1986. This decision cemented his reputation as a principled leader willing to challenge orthodoxy in defense of gender justice and secularism.

After leaving the Congress, Khan briefly joined the Janata Dal in 1989 and was elected to the Lok Sabha from the Bahraich constituency in Uttar Pradesh. He served as a Union Minister in the V.P. Singh government, holding portfolios such as Civil Aviation and Energy. However, his association with the Janata Dal was short-lived, and he later joined the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) in the 1990s, though he did not contest elections under its banner. Disillusioned with party politics, he took a hiatus from active electoral politics in the late 1990s and focused on legal practice and public speaking.

In 2004, Khan rejoined the Congress and was appointed a member of the Rajya Sabha, the upper house of Parliament, where he served until 2010. During this period, he continued to advocate for progressive reforms, including the Uniform Civil Code and women’s rights. He also served as a member of the National Integration Council and the Consultative Committee of the Ministry of Home Affairs. His legal expertise was recognized when he was appointed as a Senior Advocate in the Supreme Court of India in 2007.

Beyond politics, Khan has been a prolific writer and commentator. He has authored several books, including *"Text and Context: Quran and Contemporary Challenges"* (2010), which explores the Quran’s teachings in the context of modern social issues, and *"Of Law and Life"* (2018), a collection of his essays on law, politics, and society. His writings reflect his deep engagement with Islamic jurisprudence, constitutional law, and secularism.

In 2019, Khan’s career took a new turn when he was appointed as the Governor of Kerala by the President of India, Ram Nath Kovind, on September 6, 2019. As governor, he has been involved in several controversies, particularly over his public statements on issues such as the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) and the National Register of Citizens (NRC), which have often clashed with the views of the state government led by the Left Democratic Front (LDF). Despite the tensions, he has continued to emphasize the importance of constitutional values and national unity in his speeches.

Khan is married to Reshma Arif, and the couple has two children, a son and a daughter. His son, Omar Arif, is a lawyer, while his daughter, Sara Arif, is a journalist. Throughout his career, Khan has remained a vocal advocate for secularism, gender equality, and constitutional morality, often drawing from his legal training and personal convictions to shape his public positions. His life and work reflect a consistent commitment to reform, even at the cost of personal and political consequences.

title: Nikole Hannah-Jones
text:
Nikole Hannah-Jones was born on April 9, 1976, in Waterloo, Iowa, to Milton Hannah, an African American man originally from Greenwood, Mississippi, and Cheryl A. Novotny, a white woman of Czech and English descent. Her parents met while her father was serving in the U.S. Army, and their interracial marriage was uncommon in the 1970s, which influenced Hannah-Jones’s later work on racial inequality. She grew up in a predominantly white, working-class neighborhood in Waterloo, where she attended public schools that were racially segregated due to housing patterns. This early exposure to systemic disparities in education became a defining theme in her journalism.

Hannah-Jones graduated from Waterloo West High School in 1994 and enrolled at the University of Notre Dame, where she initially studied history and African American studies. However, financial struggles led her to transfer to the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC) in 1995, where she earned a bachelor’s degree in history and African American studies in 1998. During her time at UNC, she worked as a reporter for *The Daily Tar Heel*, the student newspaper, which sparked her interest in journalism. After graduation, she briefly worked at *The News & Observer* in Raleigh, North Carolina, before pursuing a master’s degree in mass communication at UNC’s Hussman School of Journalism and Media, which she completed in 2003.

Her professional journalism career began in earnest in 2003 when she joined *The Oregonian* in Portland, where she covered education and social issues for six years. During this time, she reported on racial disparities in school discipline and housing segregation, earning recognition for her investigative work. In 2007, she won the Sigma Delta Chi Award for Public Service Journalism from the Society of Professional Journalists for her series on the resegregation of Portland’s public schools. Her reporting also contributed to the paper’s 2006 Pulitzer Prize for Breaking News Reporting for coverage of a school shooting.

In 2011, Hannah-Jones left *The Oregonian* to join *ProPublica*, a nonprofit investigative newsroom based in New York City. There, she focused on civil rights and racial injustice, producing groundbreaking stories such as "Segregation Now," a 2014 investigation into the resegregation of public schools in Tuscaloosa, Alabama. The series won numerous awards, including the National Magazine Award for Public Interest in 2015 and the Peabody Award in 2016. Her work at *ProPublica* also included reporting on housing discrimination, which earned her the 2015 George Polk Award for National Reporting.

In 2015, Hannah-Jones was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship, often called the "Genius Grant," which provided her with $625,000 over five years to pursue her work without financial constraints. The same year, she joined *The New York Times Magazine* as a staff writer, where she continued to investigate racial inequality in education and housing. Her most notable project at the *Times* was "The 1619 Project," launched in August 2019 to mark the 400th anniversary of the arrival of the first enslaved Africans in the English colonies. The project reframed American history by centering slavery and its enduring legacy, sparking both widespread acclaim and intense political backlash. It won the 2020 Pulitzer Prize for Commentary for Hannah-Jones’s introductory essay, though the award was met with controversy, including criticism from some historians and conservative politicians.

Beyond journalism, Hannah-Jones has been a vocal advocate for racial justice and media diversity. In 2020, she was appointed the Knight Chair in Race and Journalism at the Howard University School of Communications, a historically Black university in Washington, D.C. The position was initially planned for UNC, but after a contentious debate over whether she would receive tenure—a decision delayed by political opposition—she declined the offer and accepted the role at Howard instead. The dispute highlighted broader tensions over academic freedom and racial equity in higher education.

Hannah-Jones has received numerous honors, including the National Association of Black Journalists’ Journalist of the Year Award in 2015 and 2020, and the John Chancellor Award for Excellence in Journalism from Columbia University in 2019. She has also been named to *Time* magazine’s 100 Most Influential People list in 2021. In 2021, she published *The 1619 Project: A New Origin Story*, an expanded book version of the original project, which became a *New York Times* bestseller. She continues to write, teach, and speak on issues of racial justice, education, and journalism, while also serving on the board of the Ida B.
